questions.question: A stick is 5 paperclips long, and a crayon is longer. I measure the same stick with crayons. My number will be:
questions.explain: A bigger unit covers more, so you need fewer of them and the number gets smaller. The trap is thinking a bigger unit gives a bigger number.

questions.question: You measure your book with 4 hand-spans. You must use the same hand-span each time. Why?
options: So you can add crayons too.
questions.explain: We use the same unit so every step is equal and the count is fair. Mixing different sizes in one measurement makes the count mean nothing.

questions.question: A pencil is 3 crayons long, and a paperclip is shorter. I measure with paperclips. My number will be:
questions.explain: A smaller unit covers less, so you need more of them and the number gets bigger. The trap is thinking the number stays the same no matter the unit.

questions.question: You want to measure a long table. You have small cubes and big blocks. You must use the same unit all the way. Which is right?
options: Use cubes, then switch to blocks.
Use the biggest one you find.
Use as many pieces as you can.
Pick one and use it all the way.
questions.explain: Pick one unit and keep it the same for the whole measurement. Switching units in the middle makes the count meaningless.

questions.question: You line up 7 small cubes on a stick. Then 4 big blocks on the same stick. Why is the number smaller with blocks?
questions.explain: Each big block covers more space than a small cube, so fewer blocks are needed. The number is smaller because the unit is bigger.

questions.question: You measure your bed with 2 hand-spans, then 3 crayons, then 4 fingers. Is that a good measurement?
questions.explain: You must use the same unit the whole time. Mixing hand-spans, crayons, and fingers makes the total count meaningless.

questions.question: A rope is 8 paperclips. A stick is 5 crayons, and a crayon is longer than a paperclip. Can you say which is longer?
questions.explain: You cannot compare counts made with different units. Even though a crayon is longer, you do not know exactly how much longer, so you cannot say for sure.

questions.question: You measure a desk with 4 big blocks. Your friend measures the same desk with small cubes and gets 12. What does this tell you?
options: A cube is longer than a block.
questions.explain: It takes fewer big blocks to cover the desk, so each block is longer than a cube. The trap is thinking the object with the bigger number is longer.

questions.question: Max says his pencil is 4 paperclips long and his friend pencil is 6 fingers long. He says his is shorter. What went wrong?
questions.explain: He compared 4 paperclips to 6 fingers, but those are different units so you cannot say which is longer. You must measure with the same unit to compare.

questions.question: You put 3 hand-spans end to end on your arm. A finger is shorter than a hand-span. Now you put fingers end to end on the same arm. Your number will be:
questions.explain: A finger is shorter, so more fingers fit on the same arm. The trap is thinking the number stays the same or gets smaller.

questions.question: You put 6 coins end to end on a shelf. A crayon is longer than a coin. You put crayons end to end on the same shelf. The crayon number will be:
questions.explain: A crayon is longer, so fewer crayons fit on the same shelf. The trap is thinking a bigger unit gives a bigger number.

questions.question: You want to measure a long rope. You have small coins and big crayons. You can only use one kind. Which should you pick to get a smaller number?
questions.explain: Bigger units give a smaller number because fewer of them fit. The trap is picking the small coins or mixing them.

questions.question: You put 4 crayons end to end on a ruler. A paperclip is shorter than a crayon. You put paperclips end to end on the same ruler. Your number will be:
questions.explain: A paperclip is shorter, so more of them fit on the same ruler. The trap is thinking the number gets smaller or stays the same.

questions.question: You are measuring a rope. You put 3 cubes, then 2 blocks, then 4 coins. You say the rope is 9. What is wrong?
questions.explain: You cannot mix cubes, blocks, and coins because they are different sizes. The trap is thinking you can just add the numbers together.

questions.question: You measure a rope with 5 hand-spans. Your sister measures the same rope with 10 fingers. You both measured the same rope. Why did you get different numbers?
questions.explain: A hand-span and a finger are different sizes, so different numbers are expected. The trap is thinking one number is wrong or adding them together.
